title: Unique Paths
description:
# Unique Paths

A robot is on an `m x n` grid. It starts at the top-left cell and wants to reach the bottom-right cell. At any step, the robot may move only **right** or **down**.

Return the number of different paths from the start to the destination.

A path is determined by the order of its right and down moves. The robot never moves up or left, so there are no cycles.

## Example 1:

**Input:** m = 3, n = 7
**Output:** 28

## Example 2:

**Input:** m = 3, n = 2
**Output:** 3
**Explanation:** The three move orders are RDD, DRD, and DDR.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= m, n <= 100`
* The answer is at most `2 * 10^9` for every test case.

solutions.name: Two-Dimensional Grid DP
solutions.description:
## Approach
Create a table where `dp[row][col]` is the number of ways to reach that cell from the start. The first row and first column are all 1 because there is only one straight-line route to those cells. Every other cell receives paths from above and from the left.

## Key Insight
Because the robot only moves right or down, the path graph is acyclic and each cell depends only on two already-computed parents. The recurrence is `dp[row][col] = dp[row - 1][col] + dp[row][col - 1]`.

## Complexity Analysis
The algorithm fills every grid cell once, so the time complexity is O(m * n). The full table uses O(m * n) space.

solutions.name: One-Row Rolling DP
solutions.description:
## Approach
Store only the current row. `dp[col]` already holds the number of ways from the cell above, while `dp[col - 1]` is the number of ways from the left in the current row. Add them to update the current cell.

## Key Insight
The full table recurrence needs only the previous row and current left neighbor. Since `dp[col]` is updated left to right, one row of memory is enough.

## Complexity Analysis
The nested loops still visit every grid cell, so the time complexity is O(m * n). The rolling row has length n, so the space complexity is O(n).

solutions.name: Top-Down Memoized Grid Walk
solutions.description:
## Approach
Define `paths(row, col)` as the number of ways to reach the destination from that cell. From a non-terminal cell, recurse down and right, then memoize the result.

## Key Insight
Once the robot reaches the last row or last column, there is exactly one straight path left. Memoization prevents the same grid suffix from being recomputed through many different prefixes.

## Complexity Analysis
Each grid cell becomes one memoized state, so the time complexity is O(m * n). The memo table and recursion stack use O(m * n) space in the worst case.

solutions.name: Multiplicative Combinatorics
solutions.description:
## Approach
Every path has exactly `m - 1` down moves and `n - 1` right moves, for `m + n - 2` total moves. Choose the positions of the smaller move group and compute the binomial coefficient multiplicatively.

## Key Insight
The grid path is equivalent to arranging a fixed multiset of moves. Multiplicative computation avoids building large factorials and keeps intermediate values controlled with `long`.

## Complexity Analysis
The loop runs `min(m - 1, n - 1)` times, so the time complexity is O(min(m, n)). Only a few scalar variables are used, so the space complexity is O(1).

solutions.name: DAG Path Count Propagation
solutions.description:
## Approach
Treat the grid as a directed acyclic graph. Put one way at the start cell, then scan cells in row-major order and push each cell's path count to its down and right neighbors.

## Key Insight
Instead of asking how many paths enter a cell, this route pushes known path counts forward along outgoing edges. It teaches the same recurrence as graph path counting on a DAG.

## Complexity Analysis
Each cell is processed once and each cell has at most two outgoing edges, so the time complexity is O(m * n). The `ways` grid uses O(m * n) space.

tests.description: Canonical 3 by 7 grid has twenty-eight right/down paths.
Narrow 3 by 2 grid verifies the recurrence on a small rectangle.
Swapped dimensions should produce the same number of paths by symmetry.
Square 3 by 3 grid has six routes.
Single-cell grid already starts at the destination.
One-row grid has only one path moving right.
One-column grid has only one path moving down.
Larger square grid checks that the combinatorics route handles bigger counts.
Smallest grid that requires a choice between two paths.
Thin rectangle verifies the exact move-order counting.
Medium square grid catches off-by-one errors in row and column counts.
Large square grid still fits the promised answer bound.
Large asymmetric grid checks multiplicative binomial arithmetic.
